questions.text:
Consider a network with three routers P, Q, R shown in the figure below. All the links have cost of unity.

The routers exchange distance vector routing information and have converged on the routing tables, after which the link Q-R fails. Assume that P and Q send out routing updates at random times, each at the same average rate. The probability of a routing loop formation (rounded off to one decimal place) between P and Q, leading to count-to-infinity problem, is ____
questions.solution:
Before failure: Q reaches R at cost 1, P reaches R at cost 2 (via Q). After Q-R fails:
- If Q sends its update first (R unreachable), P learns R is unreachable [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] no loop.
- If P sends first, it still advertises "R at cost 2". Q then sets its route to R via P (cost 3), and P routes through Q [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] routing loop and count-to-infinity.

Both are equally likely, so probability [latex]=0.5[/latex].

Answer: 0.5

questions.text:
Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be a directed graph, where [latex]V = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \}[/latex] is the set of vertices and [latex]E[/latex] is the set of directed edges, as defined by the following adjacency matrix [latex]A[/latex].
[latex]A[i][j]= \left \{ \begin{matrix} 1 &1 \leq j \leq i \leq 5 \\ 0& otherwise \end{matrix} \right.[/latex]
[latex]A[i][j]=1 [/latex]indicates a directed edge from node [latex]i [/latex] to node [latex]j [/latex]. A directed spanning tree of [latex]G [/latex], rooted at [latex] r \in V[/latex] , is defined as a subgraph [latex]T [/latex] of [latex]G [/latex] such that the undirected version of [latex]T [/latex] is a tree, and [latex]T [/latex] contains a directed path from [latex]r [/latex] to every other vertex in [latex]V [/latex]. The number of such directed spanning trees rooted at vertex 5 is ____
questions.solution:
Edge [latex]i\rightarrow j[/latex] exists only when [latex]j\le i[/latex], so edges go from larger to smaller vertices (self-loops are useless in a tree).

In a tree rooted at 5, each other vertex k needs exactly one parent, which must be a vertex larger than k:
- vertex 4: parent 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1 choice
- vertex 3: 4 or 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 choices
- vertex 2: 3 choices
- vertex 1: 4 choices

Parents are always larger, so no cycle can form. Total [latex]=1\times2\times3\times4=24[/latex]

Answer: 24

questions.text: Consider a 100 Mbps link between an earth station (sender) and a satellite (receiver) at an altitude of 2100 km. The signal propagates at a speed of [latex]3  \times 10^8[/latex] m/s. The time taken (in milliseconds, rounded off to two decimal places) for the receiver to completely receive a packet of 1000 bytes transmitted by the sender is
questions.solution:
Total time = transmission time + propagation time.
- Transmission time [latex]=\frac{1000\times8}{100\times10^6}=0.08[/latex] ms
- Propagation time [latex]=\frac{2100\times10^3}{3\times10^8}=7[/latex] ms

Total [latex]=0.08+7=7.08[/latex] ms

Answer: 7.08

questions.text: Consider the data transfer using TCP over a 1 Gbps link. Assuming that the maximum segment lifetime (MSL) is set to 60 seconds, the minimum number of bits required for the sequence number field of the TCP header, to prevent the sequence number space from wrapping around during the MSL is
questions.solution:
TCP numbers bytes. Bytes sent in one MSL:
[latex]\frac{10^9\times60}{8}=7.5\times10^9[/latex] bytes

We need [latex]2^k\ge7.5\times10^9[/latex]. [latex]2^{32}\approx4.29\times10^9[/latex] (too small), [latex]2^{33}\approx8.59\times10^9[/latex] (enough).

Answer: 33
